symptoms: Dark brown to black circular lesions on older lower leaves displaying distinct concentric target-like rings
Yellow chlorotic zone surrounds expanding lesions as pathogen produces alternaric acid
Stems develop dark, sunken, concentric lesions (collar rot in young transplants)
Fruit develops sunken, leathery dark spots at the stem end with concentric rings
management: Prune off heavily infected lower foliage (up to 30cm above soil) to minimize fungal spore splash from the soil.
Water exclusively at root level with drip lines; avoid splashing soil onto leaves.
Stake or trellis plants and prune suckers to optimize air circulation and accelerate drying.
Consult local agrovet and extension officers for PCPB-registered protectant or systemic fungicides when disease pressure is persistent.
prevention: Apply organic or plastic mulch around plant bases to prevent soil splash onto lower canopy.
Rotate fields out of Solanaceae crops for a minimum of 2-3 years.
Select tolerant tomato varieties where available in the Kenyan market.
Sanitize pruning knives and stakes between crop cycles.
monitoring: Inspect the bottom leaves weekly, particularly after high humidity, morning dews, or intermittent rain.
Track whether lesions begin spreading up into the middle fruiting canopy.
escalation: Target spots progress past lower leaves into the cluster and flower zone.
Lesions detected on green or ripening fruit stems.
Defoliation exposes ripening fruit to sunscald.
kenya_notes: Ubiquitous in open-field tomato production across Kenya. Heaviest during warm, humid transition periods between rains. Staking and mulching reduce disease severity by over 50%.
